turns.doctor_question: Hello, I'm Dr. Smith. It's nice to meet you; could you tell me what brings you in to see me today?
turns.patient_response:
I guess they brought me in because... well, at the warehouse where I work, I keep doing things. Like, I'll just freeze with my arms up right by the forklift. Which is weird because I actually know how to drive the forklift, I learned how back before I dropped out of my college classes. I was studying business for a little bit, but the textbooks were just way too expensive and heavy. 

Anyway, I stand there by the forklift and I start copying the beeping sounds it makes when it backs up, and doing all the hand signals. And moving the boxes in these strange little patterns. Even when everyone is yelling for me to stop, I just... I keep doing the patterns. The boxes are mostly just regular cardboard, obviously, but sometimes they get this weird packing tape on them that smells exactly like vinegar. I really hate vinegar. My mom used to clean our living room windows with vinegar and newspaper when I was a kid, and it just leaves streaks everywhere, you know? It doesn't even work that well. But yeah, my boss said I had to come see you because of the box patterns and the beeping.

symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient exhibits tangential speech, drifting from the forklift to college textbooks, and from cardboard boxes to the smell of vinegar and childhood window cleaning.
symptom_reasoning.S022: The patient describes freezing with their arms up (posturing), copying beeping sounds (echolalia), copying hand signals (echopraxia), and moving boxes in strange patterns (stereotypy).

turns.doctor_question: Have you been feeling unusually high-spirited or energetic, or perhaps quite low or hopeless, for a significant period of time?
turns.patient_response: No, not really. I mean, I don't feel like I have too much energy or anything. Sometimes I get tired, but that's just because the warehouse is so big. Have you ever been in one of those huge distribution centers? The ceiling is so high, it's like an airplane hangar. I went to an airshow once with my dad when I was maybe ten or eleven. They had these old World War II planes, the ones with the propellers on the front, and the noise they make is so loud you can feel it in your teeth. My dad bought me this little model plane, but I accidentally stepped on it in the parking lot and broke one of the wings off. It was painted this really bright yellow color. I still have the broken wing somewhere in my desk drawer at home, right next to all these old batteries I keep forgetting to throw away. But yeah, my energy is just normal, I guess. I don't feel super sad or anything either.

symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient's speech exhibits tangentiality, drifting far off-topic from their energy levels to warehouses, airplane hangars, an airshow, a model plane, and old batteries.
symptom_reasoning.S024: The patient explicitly denies feeling 'super sad or anything'.
symptom_reasoning.S033: The patient answers 'No, not really' to the doctor's question about feeling unusually high-spirited.
symptom_reasoning.S034: The patient explicitly states they do not feel like they have too much energy and that their energy is normal.
symptom_reasoning.S083: The patient answers 'No, not really' to the doctor's question about feeling quite low or hopeless.

turns.doctor_question: Do you ever hear voices or sounds that other people around you cannot hear?
turns.patient_response: Voices? No, I don't think so. Just the normal warehouse noises, you know? The conveyer belts, the forklifts... the forklifts are electric now, mostly, which is supposed to be better for the environment. I read this article once about how lithium batteries are going to be a huge problem in like twenty years because nobody knows how to recycle them properly. It's just going to be mountains of toxic batteries. Kind of like how we used to think plastic was this amazing miracle invention, and now it's in the ocean and in fish and everything. I try to buy my groceries in glass jars when I can, but pasta sauce is so expensive when it comes in glass. You ever notice that? The plastic jars are like two dollars cheaper. But I guess you're a doctor, so you probably make enough money to buy the glass jars. My mom used to save all the glass jars and use them to store nails and screws in the garage. She'd nail the lids to the bottom of the shelves so you could just unscrew the jar from the bottom. It was actually a really smart system, until the shelf broke one day and there was glass and screws everywhere. Took us three days to sweep it all up. But no, I don't hear voices or anything like that. Just regular sounds.

symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient's response demonstrates tangentiality, wandering through a long series of loosely connected topics (forklifts, batteries, plastic, glass jars, their mother's garage) before finally returning to the original question.
symptom_reasoning.S020: The patient explicitly denies hearing voices or sounds that others cannot hear.

turns.doctor_question: Have you been experiencing any physical health issues, such as a high fever, recent head injury, or any new medical conditions that your primary care doctor has been treating you for lately?
turns.patient_response: No, I haven't been sick or anything. I haven't had a fever. I did get a really bad sunburn on my neck last weekend, though. I was out helping my neighbor move this giant pile of gravel from his driveway to his backyard. He's building this fire pit thing. It's supposed to look like those fancy ones you see in home improvement magazines, but he's just using cinder blocks and some old bricks he found. We used a wheelbarrow, and the wheel kept squeaking. It sounded exactly like this rusty gate at my elementary school. I used to swing on that gate while waiting for the bus, until Mr. Henderson, the janitor, yelled at me because I guess it bent the hinges. He was always yelling about something. He had this enormous mustache that looked like a caterpillar. But anyway, no, my head is fine, no injuries or anything. I just need to remember to put aloe on my neck because it's starting to peel.

symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient's speech exhibits tangentiality and loose associations, drifting from a sunburn to a wheelbarrow, a rusty school gate, and a janitor's mustache before returning to the original question.

turns.doctor_question: When you find yourself standing still and performing those patterns with your hands, do you feel like you are choosing to do them, or does it feel like your body is stuck and you are unable to move or stop even if you try?
turns.patient_response:
I don't know if I feel stuck, exactly. It's more like... well, I guess that's why they brought me in here, honestly. Because at the warehouse, I'll just be working and then I freeze with my arms up right by the forklift. And I start copying the beeping sounds it makes when it backs up, and doing these hand signals, or I'll start moving the boxes around in these strange little patterns. Even when everyone is yelling for me to stop, I just keep doing it. 

The foreman, Gary, he yells the loudest out of everyone. He always wears this neon orange safety vest that's way too small for him, so he looks exactly like a giant traffic cone when he gets mad and his face turns red. We stole a traffic cone once, me and my friends back in high school, and we stuck it on the very top of the flagpole out front. The principal was so mad. He made the whole senior class sit in the gym on those awful wooden bleachers until someone confessed. Nobody ever did, though. We just sat there for hours. My back was killing me by the end of it. They actually had to call the fire department to get the cone down because the school's ladder wasn't tall enough. The fire truck had one of those huge ladders that extends all the way out, you know? It took them like five minutes to hook it up. I always thought it would be cool to drive a fire truck, but you have to pass all these tests for it.

symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient's speech demonstrates tangentiality and loose associations, drifting from the foreman's vest to a high school prank with a traffic cone, and then to fire trucks.
symptom_reasoning.S022: The patient describes freezing with their arms up, copying forklift beeping sounds, and moving boxes in strange patterns despite being told to stop, indicating posturing, echolalia, and stereotypy.

turns.doctor_question: Have you ever been told by a doctor that you have any neurological issues, such as seizures, tremors, or unusual reflexes?
turns.patient_response:
No, no doctor's ever told me anything like that. No seizures or anything. I don't really go to the doctor much anyway, mostly just for those physicals they make you do for work sometimes. They always check your reflexes with that little rubber hammer, you know? Tap your knee and your leg kicks up. It's weird how your body just does that without you telling it to. 

I actually bought one of those hammers at a garage sale once. It was in this box of old medical stuff, like a stethoscope and some weird metal tools that looked like they belonged in a horror movie. The guy selling it said his grandfather was a country doctor back in the fifties. He used to drive around in this beautiful old Chevy truck, making house calls. You don't see that anymore, doctors coming to your house. Now you have to sit in those waiting rooms with the old magazines. I found a National Geographic from like 2014 in a waiting room once. It had this whole article about deep sea creatures, those fish with the little glowing lights on their heads? Anglerfish. They look terrifying, honestly, but it's pretty amazing how they survive down there where it's completely pitch black. I tried to watch a documentary about the ocean once, but I fell asleep. The narrator's voice was just so soothing, like... like he was reading a bedtime story or something. But yeah, no neurological stuff or anything like that. Just the regular knee tap thing.

symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient's response exhibits tangentiality and derailment, drifting from reflexes to a garage sale, a country doctor, waiting rooms, National Geographic, and deep sea creatures before finally returning to the original question.

turns.doctor_question: Have your friends or family mentioned that your personality has changed or that you have been acting differently in ways other than these episodes at work?
turns.patient_response: I mean, not really? My mom hasn't said anything about me acting different. She just worries about me eating enough, honestly. She came over on Sunday and brought this massive lasagna in one of those flimsy aluminum pans. You know the ones you get at the grocery store? You have to hold them from the bottom or they just buckle right in the middle. I actually dropped one of her casseroles like that a couple years ago when I lived in the dorms for a bit. It went everywhere. The carpet in that dorm was this horrible scratchy gray stuff, kind of like the material they use on speaker boxes in the trunks of cars. My buddy Jason had these two huge subwoofers in his Honda Civic back then. The bass was so loud it would literally rattle your teeth in your skull. We used to drive around the Walmart parking lot at like midnight just blasting music because there was nothing else to do in that town. They ended up putting in all these speed bumps in that parking lot, though. Like, the really aggressive yellow ones that scrape the bottom of your car if you go over three miles an hour. Jason was so mad because his car was lowered and it messed up his exhaust. But yeah, Jason hasn't said I'm acting weird or anything either. Nobody has. Just the stuff at the warehouse with the forklift and the boxes, that's all anybody talks about.

symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient's response demonstrates tangentiality and loose associations, drifting from his mother's lasagna to aluminum pans, dorm carpets, speaker boxes, his friend's car subwoofers, and speed bumps before returning to the original question.
